title: Apple’s Ternus era begins as Nvidia bets on the whole AI stack
content:
It’s officially the Ternus era at Apple.
Tim Cook stepped down as CEO this week, handing the company to former hardware chief John Ternus, whose first memo promised a “huge launch next week” — timing that puts Apple’s next iPhone event on his desk before he’s even settled in. Cook isn’t going far, though: he’s staying on as Executive Chairman, focused on the kind of policy relationships that recently turned something as small as a map label into a very public balancing act. All of which raises an obvious question: what does the Ternus era look like, and how much rope will shareholders give him to figure it out? 
 
On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, hosts Kirsten Korosec and Sean O’Kane unpack what Ternus is walking into, why he may actually be better positioned to make progress on software than hardware in this new AI era, and more of the week’s news. 
Listen to the full episode to hear more about:
- Why Nvidia keeps making moves that look less like a chipmaker and more like a company trying to own the entire AI stack, from its Hugging Face acquisition to its investment in MediaTek and deeper compute deals
- A chaotic week for robotaxis: Tesla’s Cybercab event, Waymo’s expansion into new cities, Zoox’s first paid rides, and what happens when these companies start competing head-to-head
- What Andreessen Horowitz’s new $1.1 billion “Machine Age” fund signals about where early-stage AI hardware bets are headed
- Why the $285 million acquisition of GoPro marks the end of an era for one of Silicon Valley’s original consumer tech darlings
Subscribe to Equity on YouTube, Apple Podcasts, Overcast, Spotify, and all the casts. You can also follow Equity on X and Threads at @EquityPod.

report.summary: Apple enters Ternus-led era after Tim Cook steps down, as Nvidia expands beyond chips to own the entire AI stack.
report.background: Apple’s leadership transition marks a pivotal moment: longtime CEO Tim Cook has stepped down, ceding control to former hardware chief John Ternus, who immediately faces a major iPhone launch. Cook remains executive chairman, focusing on policy. Ternus inherits a company where hardware leadership is no longer enough—the new AI era demands deeper software services and ecosystem integration. Meanwhile, Nvidia’s recent moves—acquiring Hugging Face, investing in MediaTek, and forging deeper compute partnerships—signal a strategic shift from pure chipmaker to a broad AI infrastructure provider. This convergence of Apple’s internal transition and Nvidia’s external expansion illustrates the industry’s pivot toward integrated AI platforms. The podcast also covers robotaxi competition, Andreessen Horowitz’s new AI hardware fund, and GoPro’s $285 million acquisition, underscoring how fast the tech landscape is shifting as AI reshapes companies, investments, and consumer devices.
key_points: John Ternus becomes Apple CEO with immediate pressure to deliver a huge product launch next week. His hardware-focused background may be less relevant than software and AI integration, forcing him to quickly adapt to an era where services and machine learning define device success.

Nvidia is aggressively building out the entire AI stack rather than relying solely on GPU sales. The Hugging Face acquisition and MediaTek investment indicate it wants to own model distribution, development platforms, and compute infrastructure, positioning itself as an end-to-end AI provider.

The robotaxi market grew chaotic this week as Tesla unveiled its Cybercab, Waymo expanded into more cities, and Zoox launched its first paid rides. These moves signal that autonomous ride-hailing is rapidly approaching commercial scale, but also that competition and regulatory scrutiny will intensify.

Andreessen Horowitz’s $1.1 billion Machine Age fund demonstrates venture capital’s conviction in early-stage AI hardware startups. Expect increased funding for robotics, edge AI, sensors, and specialized chips, as investors bet on the physical layer of artificial intelligence beyond software.

The $285 million acquisition of GoPro marks the end of an era for consumer action cameras, showing how hard it is for consumer hardware companies to survive without a clear AI advantage or massive platform scale. GoPro’s fate highlights broader consolidation pressures across Silicon Valley.

Ternus’s first memo promised a ‘huge launch next week,’ while Tim Cook stays on as executive chairman for policy and government relations. This leadership structure suggests continuity in strategy but renewed focus on execution, especially as Apple competes with Nvidia in AI-capable platforms.
report.impact: This leadership shift and Nvidia’s strategic expansion have broad implications. For Apple developers, Ternus’s era may prioritize tighter integration of on-device AI and cloud services, potentially changing how apps access machine learning capabilities. For AI developers, Nvidia’s move into the full stack—from Hugging Face’s model hub to compute platforms—could reduce fragmentation and simplify tooling, but also risk vendor lock-in. Regular users may see more polished AI features across Apple devices, but also face higher costs if Nvidia controls more of the pipeline. The robotaxi acceleration promises new mobility options, yet also raises safety and public policy debates. Overall, the AI landscape is consolidating around a few dominant players, making ecosystem choice increasingly consequential for developers and consumers alike.
report.tools: For readers tracking these trends: follow Nvidia’s publicly available AI stack components like CUDA libraries and NGC containers, along with Hugging Face’s Transformers library and datasets tooling to experiment with end-to-end AI workflows. Apple developers should watch Ternus-era software announcements at WWDC and the upcoming iPhone event—key APIs may include on-device foundation models or new Core ML features. For robotics and autonomous vehicle comparisons, monitor Waymo’s open datasets and simulation tools, plus Tesla’s FSD updates, to see how these competitive stacks evolve in practice.
